title: Most AI product specs I read are wishes written as requirements.
text: Medium Most AI product specs I read are wishes written as requirements. | by Saichithra Swaminathan | Nov, 2026 | Medium Sitemap Open in app Sign up Sign in Medium Logo Get app Write Search Sign up Sign in Saichithra Swaminathan Product Strategy AI Ai Evals Most AI product specs I read are wishes written as requirements. Saichithra Swaminathan 4 min read · Nov 4, 2026 -- 1 Listen Share “The assistant should give helpful, accurate, on-brand answers.” Every PRD says something like this, and you can’t test a word of it. With deterministic software you could get away with a vague spec, because the code did exactly what it did and QA could confirm it. AI features don’t work that way. The same input can give a different output tomorrow. “Helpful” means one thing to the engineer who tuned the prompt and another to the customer reading the answer. So the real spec of an AI feature isn’t the document. It’s the set of examples you test against and the criteria you use to judge them. If product doesn’t own that, someone else is setting the quality bar without saying so. 1. Quality Is a Distribution, Not a Checkbox A traditional feature either works or it doesn’t. An AI feature works most of the time, in most situations, for most users. That’s uncomfortable, and pretending otherwise is how teams ship demos rather than products. The useful question changes from “does it work?” to “how often is it good enough, and how bad is it when it isn’t?” What share of responses would we be happy to put in front of a sceptical customer? What does the worst 5% look like? Which failures are embarrassing, and which are actually harmful? You can’t answer those from a demo. A demo shows you the best run. Customers get all of them. 2. Examples Beat Adjectives “Concise” is an adjective. Twenty real inputs, each with a good answer and a bad one, is a spec. When I ask a team to define quality, I ask for examples before any principles. Writing examples makes the disagreements show up early. One person’s “concise” turns out to be another’s “unhelpfully curt”. Better to find that out in a review than in a support ticket. A decent starting eval set has: Common cases, the everyday requests that carry most of the value Edge cases, ambiguous, incomplete or badly worded inputs Adversarial cases, inputs designed to make the feature misbehave Cases where it should decline, and what a good refusal looks like If you can’t write these, you don’t yet understand the problem well enough to build for it. 3. The Rubric Is the Product Decision Every eval needs a judge: a person, a script or another model. Whichever you use, it applies a rubric, and the rubric is where your product decisions live. Does accuracy beat tone? Is a cautious “I don’t know” better than a confident partial answer? Does speed matter more than completeness? These are trade-offs, and they belong to the product leader. If you leave them to whoever writes the grading prompt, you’ve handed over product strategy without noticing. Write the rubric in plain language that a new hire could apply. If two reviewers can’t score the same answer the same way, your rubric is too vague to steer the product. 4. Evals Make Change Safe The quiet benefit of a good eval set is speed. Models change, prompts change, vendors change. Without evals, every change is a leap of faith followed by anxious watching of complaints. With them, you can try a cheaper model, a new prompt or a different approach and know within hours whether quality went up or down. Teams without evals tend to freeze, because any change might break something they can’t see. Teams with evals keep iterating, because they can see what broke. 5. Production Is Where the Spec Grows Up Your first eval set is a guess. Real usage will show you cases you never thought of. The discipline is feeding them back: every notable failure in production becomes a new test case. Over time the eval set becomes a record of everything the product has learnt about its users. Ask regularly: Which recent failures aren’t yet in the eval set? Which test cases no longer reflect how customers actually use the product? Is our pass rate rising because quality improved, or because the tests got easier? What This Is Not It isn’t a job you can hand to data science. They can build the harness, but product has to define what good looks like. It isn’t one headline accuracy number. One averaged score hides the failures that matter. It isn’t a launch gate you set once and forget. An eval set that never changes slowly stops matching the product. It isn’t a replacement for talking to customers. Evals tell you whether you hit the target. Customers tell you whether it was the right target. The Shift for Product Leaders For years the PM’s main artefact was the requirements document. For AI features it’s becoming a living set of examples and judgements. That isn’t a step down into technical detail. It’s the clearest product thinking we’re asked for, because it forces us to say exactly what good means. Here’s a simple test. Pick any AI feature your team runs and ask: “If the model changed tonight, how would we know by tomorrow whether it got better or worse?” If the answer is “we’d wait for complaints”, you don’t have a spec.
